name: Mormonism
info: Mormonism is the theology and religious tradition of the Latter Day Saint movement, a Restorationist Christian movement started by Joseph Smith in Western New York in the 1820s and 1830s and known for the Book of Mormon.

facts.origin: Western New York, in the 1820s and 1830s, during the religious excitement of the Second Great Awakening; Smith said he received a vision in the spring of 1820 and organised the Church of Christ in 1830.
facts.founder: Joseph Smith, whom his followers saw as a modern-day prophet; after his killing in 1844 a succession crisis split the movement, and the largest group followed Brigham Young.
facts.scriptures: The Bible (the Authorized King James Version in the LDS Church), the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price; the Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible has varying acceptance among denominations.
facts.followers: The LDS Church claimed a membership of 16 million in 2020; no total is given for the whole movement, from which one source estimates over 400 denominations have sprung.

t: Mormons believe that God the Father, Jesus Christ and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings, that Jesus's atonement saves all people, and that the faithful may attain godhood in the afterlife.

Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon in 1830, which he said he had translated from golden plates, and organised the Church of Christ the same year; after he was killed in 1844 the largest group followed Brigham Young to Utah.

The Utah-based LDS Church banned plural marriage in 1890 and grew from about 1.7 million members in 1960 to a claimed 16 million in 2020, while over 400 denominations are estimated to have sprung from the movement.
dyk: In the Mormon account of the pre-earthly life, all people first existed as spirits or "intelligences" in the presence of God, and a "third" of them, led by Satan, rejected his plan of salvation.
ev: Joseph Smith says that God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision and told him to join none of the existing churches
Smith publishes the Book of Mormon and formally organises the Church of Christ
Mormons are expelled from Jackson County, Missouri, and flee to other parts of the state
After fighting between Missourians and Mormons, the governor of Missouri issues an "extermination order" and the Mormons flee the state
Smith is killed by a mob, precipitating a succession crisis; the largest group follows Brigham Young to what became the Utah Territory
Church president Wilford Woodruff announces the official end of plural marriage in the Manifesto
The LDS Church abandons the exclusion of black men from the priesthood
The LDS Church claims a membership of 16 million

sections.origins:
Mormonism is the theology and religious tradition of the Latter Day Saint movement, a form of Restorationist Christianity started by Joseph Smith in Western New York in the 1820s and 1830s, during a period of religious excitement known as the Second Great Awakening. Smith, then a 14-year-old farmboy, wanted to know which church taught the true doctrine of God. He said that in the spring of 1820, after praying about which denomination to join, he received the "First Vision", in which God the Father and his son Jesus Christ appeared to him and told him to join none of the existing churches. During the 1820s he chronicled several angelic visitations, and the angels told him that God would use him to re-establish the "true Christian church."

Smith said an angel first showed him the place where golden plates were buried in a nearby hill in 1823, and that he obtained them in 1827. He began dictating the Book of Mormon in April 1828 with the help of Martin Harris and later Oliver Cowdery, and finished the manuscript in June 1829. He said the plates were then returned to the angel. He began baptising new converts in 1829, published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and formally organised the Church of Christ in the same year. His followers saw him as a modern-day prophet.
sections.beliefs:
In what is called orthodox Mormonism, formalised in 1915, God the Father is called Elohim, and the Godhead is a council of three distinct divine persons: the Father, Jesus, his firstborn Son, whom Latter Day Saints call Jehovah, and the Holy Ghost. Latter Day Saints believe that the Father and Jesus have perfected, glorified, physical bodies, while the Holy Ghost is a spirit. They also believe in other gods and goddesses outside the Godhead, such as a Heavenly Mother married to God the Father, and that faithful Latter-day Saints may attain godhood in the afterlife. Mormonism does not hold the Nicene Creed's doctrine that the three are of one substance, and teaches that God organised the world from existing matter and did not create it from nothing.

Mormons believe that all people first existed as spirits in the presence of God, who proposed a plan of salvation; a "third" of them, led by Satan, rejected it. The central part of the plan is the atonement of Jesus Christ, accepted through faith, repentance, ordinances such as baptism and a Christ-like life. Mormons hold that the afterlife has three degrees of glory, and that hell, often called spirit prison, is a temporary place for the wicked between death and the resurrection. They also hold that a "Great Apostasy" corrupted the early Christian church and that priesthood authority was restored through Smith, when angels including Peter, James, John and John the Baptist appeared to him.
sections.texts:
Mormons believe in the Old and New Testaments, and the LDS Church uses the Authorized King James Version as its official Bible text. They hold the Bible to be generally accurate but incomplete, with errors introduced. The Book of Mormon, which Mormons hold to be divine scripture equal in authority to the Bible, describes itself as a chronicle of early Indigenous peoples of the Americas and their dealings with God. It begins with the departure from Jerusalem of the family of a prophet named Lehi, in the 7th century BCE, and their sailing to the Americas. It tells of Jesus visiting them after his resurrection and of their eventual loss of Christianity after generations of wars and apostasy. Smith said he translated it from "reformed Egyptian" into English.

The canon also includes the Doctrine and Covenants, which contains doctrine and prophecy, and the Pearl of Great Price, which addresses briefly Genesis to Exodus. These books and the Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible have varying degrees of acceptance among the denominations of the Latter Day Saint movement. Smith's cosmology is laid out mostly in his later revelations and sermons, particularly the Book of Abraham, the Book of Moses and the King Follett discourse. Under the principle of continuous revelation, Mormons believe that Smith and later leaders could speak scripture when moved upon by the Holy Ghost.
sections.spread:
The first Mormons met criticism and persecution from residents of Palmyra, New York and several surrounding towns when they began to organise. To avoid confrontation, Smith and the early members moved west to Kirtland, Ohio, and Jackson County, Missouri, where they hoped to establish a permanent New Jerusalem or City of Zion. They were expelled from Jackson County in 1833 and fled to other parts of Missouri. In 1838 fighting between Missourians and Mormons led the governor of Missouri to issue an "extermination order", forcing them to flee the state. In Illinois the church bought a small town, renamed it Nauvoo, and lived there with a degree of peace and prosperity for a few years, until tensions with its neighbours escalated again.

After Smith was killed by a mob in 1844, the largest group followed Brigham Young and emigrated to what became the Utah Territory, where the church began the open practice of plural marriage. Polygamy was also a major cause of opposition to Mormonism in Idaho and Arizona. The LDS Church grew rapidly in the latter half of the 20th century, from about 1.7 million members in 1960 to around 7.7 million in 1990; growth has since slowed, and the church claimed 16 million members in 2020. Groups split from the movement as early as 1831, and one source estimates that over 400 denominations have sprung from it.
sections.community:
Members of the LDS Church consider their top leaders prophets and apostles and are encouraged to accept their positions on theology, while seeking confirmation through personal study and prayer. Personal revelation is expected: parents, individuals and church officers are held to be entitled to inspiration for their own responsibilities. The church keeps a degree of orthodoxy by excommunicating or disciplining members who take positions or engage in practices viewed as apostasy, among them polygamy and the adoption of Mormon fundamentalism. Ordination to the priesthoods is for males, and black men were excluded from the priesthood until the LDS Church abandoned the exclusion in 1978.

Members receive patriarchal blessings declaring their lineage within one of the tribes of Israel, by blood or by adoption at baptism. Polygamy was the faith's most sensational characteristic in the 19th century, and vigorous opposition by the United States Congress threatened the church's existence as a legal institution. The Utah-based LDS Church banned it in 1890, and statehood for Utah soon followed. Groups that broke away after the end of plural marriage formed Mormon fundamentalist denominations, which teach that plural marriage is required for exaltation. The Community of Christ, formerly the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, is the second-largest Latter Day Saint denomination and is Trinitarian.
sections.legacy:
Mormonism describes itself as part of world Christianity but as a distinct restored dispensation, and nearly all Mormons identify as Christian. For some who define Christianity by the doctrines of Catholicism, Eastern and Oriental Orthodoxy, the Churches of the East and Protestantism, its differences place it outside Christianity. In the 1830s many American Christians came to view its early doctrines as politically and culturally subversive and doctrinally heretical, which led to a series of sometimes deadly conflicts; such violence declined in the 20th century, though its views still draw criticism. Much of its belief system is oriented around the Americas: Mormons hold that the peoples of the Book of Mormon lived in the Western Hemisphere and that the New Jerusalem will be built in Missouri.

In the 1990s Jewish groups opposed baptism for the dead on behalf of Jewish victims of the Holocaust; Mormons believe the dead may accept or reject the ordinance. Criticism of the LDS Church has concerned plural marriage, historical revisionism, racism, sexist policies, financial disclosure and the historical authenticity of the Book of Mormon. Since 2018 the LDS Church has pushed to distance itself from the label Mormonism, while cultural Mormons identify with the culture, especially in the American West, without necessarily sharing the theology.

summary: Mormonism is the tradition of the Latter Day Saint movement, started by Joseph Smith in Western New York in the 1820s and 1830s. Its followers hold the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price as scripture alongside the Bible. The largest body, the LDS Church, followed Brigham Young to Utah and claimed 16 million members in 2020.
references: Samuel Morris Brown, In Heaven as It Is on Earth: Joseph Smith and the Early Mormon Conquest of Death (Oxford University Press, 2012)
Steven L. Shields, Divergent Paths of the Restoration: a History of the Latter Day Saint Movement (Restoration Research, 1990)
Dan Vogel, Joseph Smith: The Making of a Prophet (Signature Books, 2004)
notes: Source: the article Mormonism only. It says little of the movement's history after 1890, of its spread outside the United States and of ritual beyond the ordinances, so those parts are short.

Start 1820 (circa): the article says doctrines began in the 1820s and dates Smith's claimed First Vision to spring 1820; the Church of Christ was organised in 1830. The article does not date the earlier Mormon 'beliefs' to a single founding year.

Left out because the article is not clear: the article says the Book of Mormon was published in 1830 and also that Smith began baptising in 1829; both are given. Smith's own words in the article on the plates ('reformed Egyptian') are attributed to him.
The article gives no figure for deaths in the Missouri conflict or at Smith's killing; none is given. It calls the 1915 formalisation 'Mormon orthodoxy' based on earlier teachings.

Disputed standing: the article says Mormonism categorises itself within Christianity and nearly all Mormons identify as Christian, while some who define Christianity by creeds place it outside; both are told, with no verdict.

Left out as thin or of the present day: UFOlogy, the Jerusalem Center, Mormonism's name for Heavenly Mother in detail, Adam-God doctrine, blood atonement, the White Horse Prophecy (a fundamentalist belief officially shunned), the LGBT-friendly Restoration Church (1985-2010) and the Godbeites.

Faith map: the article gives no year for the move to Kirtland, Nauvoo or Utah; those years are mine (Kirtland 1831, Nauvoo 1839 after the 1838 order, Utah 1847 after 1844) and the editor should check them against a second source or drop them. Coordinates are from general geography.
